title: cgo & Calling C
summary: **cgo** lets Go call C code (and C call Go). You write C in a special comment above `import "C"`, and the toolchain generates the glue. It unlocks decades of C libraries — but every call crosses a boundary with real overhead, manual memory rules, and the loss of pure-Go portability, so you use it deliberately.

subtopics.title: import "C" and the preamble
subtopics.explanation: cgo is activated by importing the pseudo-package "C". The C code in the comment IMMEDIATELY above that import (the preamble) — includes, types, functions — is compiled and made callable as C.foo. There must be no blank line between the comment and import "C".

subtopics.title: Type conversions across the boundary
subtopics.explanation: Go and C have different type systems. cgo exposes C types as C.int, C.char, etc. You convert explicitly: C.int(x), and use helpers like C.CString (Go string -> C char*) and C.GoString (C char* -> Go string).

subtopics.title: Memory ownership & C.free
subtopics.explanation: C.CString allocates with C's malloc, NOT Go's GC. The Go garbage collector knows nothing about it, so YOU must C.free it (cast through unsafe.Pointer). Forgetting this leaks memory in the C heap.

subtopics.title: The pointer-passing rules
subtopics.explanation: Go may pass a Go pointer to C, but C must not keep it past the call's return, and you can't pass a Go pointer that itself points to Go memory containing Go pointers. These rules let the GC stay correct; cgo checks some of them at runtime (panicking on violation).

subtopics.title: Call overhead & goroutine handoff
subtopics.explanation: A cgo call is far more expensive than a Go call (tens of nanoseconds vs ~1): the runtime must switch the goroutine to a system stack and may hand it to a thread that can block in C, affecting the scheduler. Batch work across the boundary rather than calling C in a tight loop.
subtopics.example: // prefer one C call over a million

subtopics.title: Build implications (CGO_ENABLED, cross-compile)
subtopics.explanation: cgo needs a C toolchain at build time and produces binaries linked against C libraries, breaking Go's easy static cross-compilation. Setting CGO_ENABLED=0 forces pure Go (and disables cgo); many teams keep it off for portable, static binaries.
subtopics.example: CGO_ENABLED=0 go build  # pure-Go static binary

foundations.overview: Sometimes the code you need already exists in C — SQLite, libpng, a cryptographic library, a hardware SDK. cgo is Go's foreign-function interface to that world. You embed C in a comment, import the magic pseudo-package "C", and call C functions as C.foo from Go. The toolchain generates the marshaling glue. It's genuinely powerful, but it punches a hole in Go's clean model: calls are slow, memory must be managed by hand across two heaps, and your build now needs a C compiler.
foundations.formalDefinition: cgo is the Go feature and tool that enables interoperability between Go and C. Activated by `import "C"`, it compiles the C in the immediately preceding comment (the preamble), generates Go bindings for the referenced C symbols, and links the result, allowing Go to call C functions and C to call exported Go functions.
foundations.whyItMatters: cgo is how Go reuses the enormous body of mature C libraries instead of reimplementing them. But because it carries real costs — performance, portability, safety — knowing when (and when not) to use it, and how to manage the boundary correctly, is a hallmark of senior Go engineering.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of cgo as a customs checkpoint between two countries (Go and C) with different currencies (type systems) and laws (memory management). Crossing is allowed but slow: you fill out forms (type conversions), exchange currency (CString/GoString), and anything you carry into C-land you're responsible for bringing back or disposing of (C.free). Cross rarely and carry a lot each time.
foundations.runtimePerspective: A cgo call isn't a plain CALL. The runtime moves the goroutine onto a dedicated system (g0) stack because C expects a large contiguous stack, and marks the thread as potentially blocking in C so the scheduler can spin up another thread (M) to keep Go goroutines running. This handoff is why a cgo call costs tens of nanoseconds and why C code that blocks doesn't freeze the whole runtime — but it does tie up an OS thread.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Database drivers (mattn/go-sqlite3), image/audio codecs, crypto bindings (older OpenSSL wrappers), GPU and ML runtimes, and hardware/OS APIs with no pure-Go equivalent.
foundations.businessImpact: cgo lets a team ship features in days by binding a battle-tested C library instead of spending months reimplementing it — but it can complicate CI, containers, and cross-platform releases, raising operational cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: It introduces a C build dependency, weakens static analysis and the race detector across the boundary, and makes crashes able to come from C (segfaults) rather than Go panics. Many teams prefer pure-Go alternatives precisely to avoid this.
foundations.performanceImpact: Per-call overhead is large relative to native Go, so cgo is great for coarse-grained calls (process a whole buffer) and terrible in tight inner loops; profile and batch across the boundary.
commonUseCases: Binding a mature C library (SQLite, libpng, zlib)
Hardware/OS APIs with no Go equivalent
Calling vendor SDKs shipped as C

commonMisconceptions.myth: cgo calls are about as cheap as Go calls.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They cost tens of nanoseconds and involve a goroutine/stack handoff — orders of magnitude more than a Go call. Never call C in a hot inner loop.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go's GC frees memory returned by C.CString.
commonMisconceptions.reality: C.CString uses C's malloc; the Go GC never touches it. You must C.free it yourself or it leaks.
cgo requires a C toolchain and links against C libraries, breaking trivial static cross-compilation; CGO_ENABLED=0 disables it for portable binaries.

visualExplorer.title: What happens during a cgo call
visualExplorer.caption: Crossing from Go into C and back, step by step.

config.intro: The lifecycle of a single C.foo() call:

steps.name: Convert arguments
steps.detail: Go values are translated to C types (e.g. C.int(x), C.CString(s)); CString allocates on the C heap.

steps.name: Switch stacks
steps.detail: The runtime moves the goroutine onto a system (g0) stack because C expects a large contiguous stack.

steps.name: Mark thread blockable
steps.detail: The thread (M) is flagged as possibly blocking in C, so the scheduler can run other goroutines on another thread.

steps.name: Run C code
steps.detail: The C function executes; it must not retain Go pointers past return (cgo enforces some of this).

steps.name: Return & clean up
steps.detail: Results are converted back to Go types, the goroutine returns to its Go stack, and you C.free anything you allocated.

visualExplorer.title: Why a blocking C call doesn't freeze Go
visualExplorer.caption: When a goroutine enters C and might block, the runtime detaches its P from the thread so another thread can keep running Go goroutines (G) — but the blocked thread (M) stays tied up in C, which is why too many concurrent cgo calls can exhaust threads.

interactiveExamples.title: Call a C function from Go
interactiveExamples.explanation: The preamble (the comment directly above import "C") defines C code. There must be NO blank line between it and import "C". We call C.add as if it were a Go function, converting ints to C.int.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: free the C string to stop the leak
interactiveExamples.explanation: C.CString allocates with malloc; the Go GC won't free it. The starter leaks. Add a deferred C.free (through unsafe.Pointer) so the memory is released.

interactiveExamples.title: Building cgo code and toggling CGO_ENABLED
interactiveExamples.explanation: cgo needs a C compiler at build time. These commands show building a cgo program, and how CGO_ENABLED=0 forces a pure-Go static binary (which fails if the code truly needs C).

code.code:
# Normal build: requires a C toolchain (gcc/clang). cgo is on by default.
go build ./...

# Inspect what cgo generates (glue .go and .c files):
go tool cgo main.go && ls _obj/

# Force pure Go: disables cgo, produces a static, portable binary.
# Fails if any imported package actually requires cgo.
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o app .

# Cross-compile pure Go easily (no C toolchain needed):
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -o app-linux-arm64 .
code.expectedOutput:
# go build ./...        -> builds, linking against C
# CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -> static binary, or error if cgo is required
# cross-compile          -> app-linux-arm64 produced with no C toolchain

checkpoints.prompt: This cgo helper compiles and returns the right length but leaks memory on every call. Why?
options: C.CString allocates on the C heap; without C.free the memory leaks (the Go GC won't reclaim it)
You can't return an int from cgo
strings can't be passed to C
checkpoints.explanation: C.CString calls C's malloc, which the Go garbage collector knows nothing about. Each call leaks that buffer. Add `defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cs))` to release it.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is calling a C function via cgo so much more expensive than calling a Go function?
options: The runtime must switch the goroutine to a system stack and mark the thread as possibly blocking in C
cgo recompiles the C each call
checkpoints.explanation: Each cgo call performs a goroutine/stack handoff onto the system (g0) stack and flags the thread as potentially blocking in C so the scheduler can keep other goroutines running. That coordination costs tens of nanoseconds versus ~1ns for a Go call, so you batch work across the boundary.

options: Disables cgo entirely, forcing a pure-Go build (and failing if any package needs C)
checkpoints.explanation: CGO_ENABLED=0 turns cgo off, so the build uses only pure Go. This yields static, easily cross-compiled binaries with no C toolchain needed — but the build fails if any imported package genuinely requires cgo.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line that releases a C.CString allocation.
checkpoints.explanation: You free C-allocated memory with C.free, passing the pointer cast through unsafe.Pointer (C.free takes a void*). C.GoString copies it into a Go string but doesn't free the original.

codeLab.title: A leak-free C round trip
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Shout(s string) string` that uppercases a string by calling a C function and returns the result as a Go string, with NO memory leak. Use C.CString to pass in (and free it), and C.GoString to copy the result back. The harness is a normal Go test that calls Shout; it asserts correctness. (Note: cgo files can't be unit-tested in the browser — run `go test` locally.)
codeLab.expectedOutput: PASS  (ok  solution  0.01s)  — run locally with a C toolchain; cgo can't run in the browser
hints: C.CString(s) allocates a C copy of s; defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cs)) to release it.
The C function mallocs its OWN result, so you must free res too — two allocations, two frees.
C.GoString(res) copies the C string into Go-managed memory, so it's safe to free res afterward.
Both C.free calls cast through unsafe.Pointer because C.free expects a void*.

debuggingLab.title: The preamble C code is ignored
debuggingLab.symptom: Build fails with 'could not determine kind of name for C.add' even though add() is clearly defined in the comment.

brokenCode.expectedOutput: could not determine kind of name for C.add

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: cgo only treats a comment as the C preamble if it is IMMEDIATELY above `import "C"` with no blank line in between. The blank line detaches the comment, so cgo sees an import "C" with an empty preamble and can't find add — hence 'could not determine kind of name'.
commonMistakes: Leaving a blank line between the C comment and import "C".
Putting other imports or code between the preamble and import "C".
Forgetting required #include lines for the C functions used.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Remove the blank line so the comment is the immediate preamble of import "C".

theory.question: How does cgo work, and why is a cgo call much more expensive than a normal Go call?
theory.directAnswer: You import the pseudo-package "C"; the C code in the comment immediately above it (the preamble) is compiled, and cgo generates Go bindings so you call C functions as C.foo. A call is expensive because the runtime must switch the goroutine onto a system (g0) stack — C expects a large contiguous stack — and mark the thread as potentially blocking in C so the scheduler can keep other goroutines running on another thread. That coordination costs tens of nanoseconds versus roughly one for a Go call, so you batch work across the boundary rather than calling C in a tight loop.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Go's foreign-function interface to C, plus the runtime machinery that makes it safe.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To reuse mature C libraries without reimplementing them in Go.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: cgo generates marshaling glue; the runtime performs a stack switch and thread bookkeeping per call.

theory.whyImportant: Understanding the cost explains the cardinal rule: don't call C in hot loops; batch.
theory.realWorldExample: go-sqlite3 binds SQLite via cgo; queries cross the boundary, so per-row C calls are avoided in favor of bulk operations.

followUps.question: What must immediately follow the preamble comment?
followUps.answer: import "C" with no blank line between them, or cgo won't treat the comment as the C preamble.

followUps.question: Can C call back into Go?
followUps.answer: Yes, via //export comments that expose Go functions to C, with the same boundary costs and pointer rules.

theory.question: What are the memory and pointer rules when passing data between Go and C, and how do you avoid leaks?
theory.directAnswer: C.CString and similar helpers allocate on the C heap with malloc, which the Go GC never reclaims — you must C.free them yourself (cast through unsafe.Pointer), typically with defer. For pointers: Go may pass a Go pointer into C, but C must not retain it after the call returns, and you may not pass a Go pointer to memory that itself contains Go pointers. cgo enforces some of these at runtime and will panic on violation. C.GoString/C.GoBytes copy C data into Go-managed memory so the GC owns the copy.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The two-heap memory model and the GC-safety rules for crossing pointers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Go's GC can move/track only Go memory; C memory and retained Go pointers would break its invariants.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: C-allocated memory is freed manually; Go pointers passed to C are restricted so the GC stays correct.

theory.whyImportant: Leaks and GC-rule violations are the most common cgo bugs in production.
theory.realWorldExample: A driver that built C strings per query leaked the C heap until defer C.free was added.

followUps.question: Why can't C keep a Go pointer after the call?
followUps.answer: The GC may move or collect the pointed-to Go object; a retained pointer in C would dangle.

followUps.question: How do you copy C bytes safely into Go?
followUps.answer: Use C.GoBytes(ptr, length) (or C.GoString), which copies into GC-managed Go memory.

scenario.question: A Go service that wraps a C image library is slow and its container won't cross-compile to ARM in CI. You suspect cgo. How do you diagnose and decide whether to keep it?
scenario.directAnswer: First confirm the cost: profile with pprof and look for cgocall frames and time spent crossing the boundary — if the code calls C per-pixel or per-row, the overhead dominates and you batch by passing whole buffers in one call. For the build: cgo requires a C toolchain and links C libraries, which breaks simple cross-compilation; either set up a cross C toolchain (or build natively per arch) or, ideally, evaluate a pure-Go alternative and set CGO_ENABLED=0 for static, trivially cross-compiled binaries. The decision is: keep cgo only if no adequate pure-Go option exists and you batch the calls.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A diagnosis of cgo call-overhead plus its build/portability tax.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Per-call handoff cost and C linking are inherent to cgo.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: pprof reveals boundary cost; CGO_ENABLED and toolchains govern portability.

scenario.whyImportant: Weighing cgo's power against its operational cost is a real senior decision.
scenario.realWorldExample: Teams have replaced a cgo image dependency with a pure-Go decoder specifically to regain static, cross-compiled, slim containers.

followUps.question: How do you spot cgo overhead in a profile?
followUps.answer: Look for runtime.cgocall and many crossings; if the hot path is per-element C calls, batch them into fewer, larger calls.

followUps.question: Why does cgo complicate Docker images?
followUps.answer: You need the C runtime/libraries present, so you can't use a scratch/distroless base as easily; CGO_ENABLED=0 enables tiny static images.

coding.question: Write a cgo wrapper `func CRandSeed(seed uint32) int` that seeds C's srand and returns one C rand() value, with correct type conversions. Explain the boundary concerns.
coding.thoughtProcess: Include <stdlib.h> in the preamble for srand/rand. Convert the Go uint32 to C.uint for srand, call C.rand(), and convert the C.int result back to a Go int. There's no allocation here, so no C.free is needed — but the call still pays cgo overhead, and rand()'s global state is shared, so concurrent callers would race in C (a real boundary concern).
coding.lineByLine: The preamble includes <stdlib.h> so srand/rand are visible. C.uint(seed) converts the Go uint32 to C's unsigned int for srand. C.rand() returns a C.int, which we convert with int(r). No memory is allocated across the boundary, so no C.free. The subtle issue: srand/rand share global state inside C, so calling this concurrently from multiple goroutines is a data race in C the Go race detector can't see — you'd need a mutex or a thread-safe RNG.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1), but with cgo per-call overhead.

followUps.question: Why is concurrent use of this unsafe?
followUps.answer: srand/rand mutate shared global C state; concurrent goroutines race on it, and Go's -race detector can't see inside C.

followUps.question: When would no C.free be needed?
followUps.answer: When you pass/return only scalar values (ints, floats) — there's no C-heap allocation to release.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Wrap each C library behind a small, idiomatic Go package that owns all conversions, frees, and locking, so the rest of the codebase sees pure Go. Decide deliberately: prefer a pure-Go alternative when one exists.
productionDeepDive.performance: cgo calls are expensive relative to Go calls; design coarse-grained APIs that cross the boundary once with a whole buffer rather than per element. Profile with pprof for runtime.cgocall hotspots.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A blocking C call ties up an OS thread; many concurrent cgo calls can exhaust threads (GOMAXTHREADS). C global state isn't protected by Go's race detector, so guard shared C state with mutexes yourself.
productionDeepDive.reliability: C code can segfault and take the whole process down (no Go panic/recover for a C crash). Validate inputs before passing to C, respect the pointer rules to avoid GC corruption, and free all C allocations (defer).
productionDeepDive.observability: cgo crossings show up as runtime.cgocall in CPU profiles; track them. Memory leaked on the C heap won't appear in Go heap profiles — watch RSS and use C-side tools (valgrind, ASan) for C-heap leaks.
productionDeepDive.security: C dependencies bring C's vulnerability surface (buffer overflows, etc.) into your binary. Pin and audit C library versions, validate all data crossing into C, and prefer memory-safe Go where feasible.

caseStudies.problem: Provide a full SQLite database driver in Go.
caseStudies.solution: Bind the SQLite C library via cgo.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Battle-tested engine and features vs. a C build dependency and harder cross-compilation.
caseStudies.lessons: cgo unlocks mature engines fast, but the build/portability tax is real — some users switch to pure-Go SQLite ports to avoid cgo.

caseStudies.problem: Want tiny, static, easily cross-compiled container images.
caseStudies.solution: Set CGO_ENABLED=0 and avoid cgo dependencies entirely.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Lose access to some C libraries in exchange for portability and slim images.
caseStudies.lessons: Defaulting to pure Go keeps builds simple; reach for cgo only when no good Go alternative exists.

keyTakeaways: cgo calls C via the pseudo-package "C"; the comment immediately above import "C" (no blank line) is the compiled C preamble.
Each cgo call is expensive (goroutine/stack handoff, tens of ns) — design coarse APIs and never call C in tight loops.
C.CString and C-returned buffers live on the C heap; the Go GC won't free them, so C.free them yourself (defer, via unsafe.Pointer).
cgo needs a C toolchain and breaks easy static cross-compilation; set CGO_ENABLED=0 for portable pure-Go binaries, and prefer pure-Go libraries when they exist.
